title: The prince set for sacrifice
hookLine: Candakumara, marked for a sacrifice by a wicked priest, saved by truth (Jataka 542)
tomorrow: The serpent who kept the precepts

cards: A courtroom, and a judge who sells his verdicts. He is Khandahala, the king's chaplain, and whoever pays him wins.
One day a man who has been cheated walks out weeping and meets Prince Canda, who hears the case again and gives the true verdict. The crowd cheers the prince for an honest judgment.
Khandahala says nothing at all, and waits for his chance.

teach.h: A DREAM, AND A CRUEL ANSWER.
teach.b: The chance comes when the king dreams of heaven and asks Khandahala the way there.
A great sacrifice, the chaplain says: the king's own children, queens, wealthy citizens, and animals, Prince Canda among them. Canda doesn't rage.
He begs his father, reasons with him, reminds him of everything between them. The people weep in the streets.
The story lets the king waver, ordering the prisoners freed, then taken back again, as Khandahala works on his fear.
At the place of sacrifice, with the blade raised, Canda's wife speaks.
She declares the truth of her life and asks that, by that truth, the harm be stopped. And Sakka, king of the gods, comes blazing down and terrifies the king into letting them go.
The crowd turns on the chaplain, the king is driven out, and Canda is made king. Tradition pairs this tale with patience, khanti.
Canda's patience isn't silence. He speaks the whole time, clearly, without hatred, to the man about to kill him.
The story is about cruelty dressed up as a sacred duty, and it puts its hope in two things: a person who keeps pleading without hating, and words that are true.

how: The tale of Canda (also called the Khandahala Jataka) is told as an example of the perfection of patience; Buddhist ethics begins with the precept of not harming living beings.

o: a vow never to speak in anger
keeping silent when you are wronged

games.q: who did what in Canda's story: tap the pairs.
p: came down and stopped the king

s: Canda was rescued by an army
he was saved by his wife's act of truth, and by Sakka's arrival.
he wavered, freeing the prisoners and then taking them back, as the chaplain worked on his fear.
the trouble began in a courtroom
Canda overturned the chaplain's bribed verdict, and the chaplain never forgave it.

games.q: you're Prince Canda, bound for a sacrifice your father has ordered. what do you do?
o: curse your father and the chaplain.
plead with your father, clearly and without hatred.
games.why: he pleads, again and again, without hatred; it's his wife's act of truth that finally stops the sacrifice.

practice: Think of one small unkindness near you that's gone unchallenged: a joke at someone's expense, a way people talk about a coworker.
Picture saying one true sentence about it, calmly, without contempt for anyone, the way Canda pleaded, and let it settle until it sounds like you.

wordCard.voice: Khanti. Patience: what Canda, marked to die for a chaplain's grudge, kept as he pleaded without hatred, before his wife's act of truth saved him. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali khanti, patience: the perfection tradition pairs with Canda's tale.

carryVoice: Your line: saved by truth. Patience, here, was never the same as silence. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jataka 542 (Khandahala Jataka, the tale of Candakumara)
